events.text: From the top of your ridge, on the eighth night of the second month, you can see the lanterns going round. There is a temple down there and a stone pagoda, and every spring the people walk round it all night, for reasons. One of your kind went down there once. There is a song about that. You have never walked next to anything in your life, and you have never wanted to, and you lie and look at the lights going round.

choices.text: Go down in a person's shape, and walk it

effects.log: It is easier than you thought, and it fits badly. You come down through the pines on two feet with your claws in your sleeves, and at the temple gate every dog in the valley is already somewhere else.

choices.text: Stay up here. Whatever that is, it is not hunting

effects.log: You watch it until the lanterns go out. Then you go and kill something, cleanly, and you sit by it. You look down that way again on the ninth night, purely to see if they are still at it.

events.text: You do the first round in the time it takes to say so. Nobody told you that there was a speed. You go by the same old couple three times, and a whole family with a lantern, and they all draw in their elbows without looking up. A gap goes round the pagoda with you in it. A monk on the steps has been counting beads. He stops, and he looks at the gap, and he starts again from the first bead, faster.

choices.text: Try to stay behind somebody, for one whole round

effects.log: It is the hardest thing you have done this year. You pick a fat man with a bad chest. You keep treading on his heels and you have to stop, and stop again. When you are done, you are sweating, and you have thought of nothing else for an hour.

choices.text: Lap the lot of them, for the pleasure of it

effects.log: Eleven rounds, before the moon moves. It is really very good. By the end of it you have the whole of the east side to yourself, and nobody can say why they have all decided to go and buy rice cakes.

events.text: At the temple gate there is an old woman selling medicine off a mat. Deer horn, bear gall, and at the front, on a clean cloth, a jar of something grey that is the most expensive thing there. You lean down and smell it. She tells you that it is the bone of a tiger of the north ridge, and very good for the knees. You knew that tiger. He was stupid and he was a good sleeper. She gives you the price, by weight.

choices.text: Ask her how much for the whole jar, and listen to how it is done

effects.log: She tells you the whole of it, proud of the trade: who catches them, who boils, what the court pays for a good skin. You nod. You had thought that you were the one who ate things, and you are glad to have had that cleared up.

choices.text: Put your hand on the jar, and look at her

effects.log: She stops talking. Her mouth stays a little open. She does not know why, and neither of you moves for some time. You take it up the mountain, and you do not know what you meant to do with it, so you bury it in a good place.

events.text: Halfway through the night a magpie comes down on the top of the pagoda and begins to scream at you. Only you. It stays right above you all the way round the circle, and it is telling everyone. It has a great deal to say about your feet. A small boy on someone's shoulders points. "That bird is shouting at that person," he says, very clearly, and heads begin to turn, and you have very little dignity left to walk with.

choices.text: Bow to it, as you have seen them bow to officials

effects.log: You bow. It is struck silent, for the first time in its life. Then it flies off to tell the whole mountain. By spring there is not a magpie in the province who does not know, and they are all extremely pleased.

choices.text: Look up at it, once, in the way that you know

effects.log: It falls off the pagoda and catches itself a hand above the ground. It does not say anything further. Nor does anybody else, on that side. You finish your round in a large clear space, and you are not asked to the rice cakes.

events.text: Somebody is going round the wrong way. No: going round the right way, very slowly, last of all, with a lantern on a stick and a left leg that swings out from the hip. You have passed {npc} four times now. {He} does not draw in {his} elbows. On the fifth round {he} says, without turning {his} head, "You are making a wind. If you have nowhere to be, you could try this side. There is no rush. It only goes round."

choices.text: Fall in beside {him}. Try to go that slowly

effects.log: It is agony. It takes you most of the night to do one round. {He} talks about the price of hemp, and {he} has to stop at the east corner to rest, and you stop too. You have never in your life stood still next to anything that you were not going to eat.

choices.text: Go on by. You have a mountain

effects.log: You go on by, and you go up, and you are in the den by dawn. There is a person down there who is going to be walking round that pagoda for a very long time, and it has nothing whatever to do with you.

events.text: You have asked about the leg. Nobody asks about the leg. {npc} gives you a long look over the lantern. "I was ten," {he} says. "I was carrying rice to the beaters, and a tiger came through the line and took me by it, and shook me, and let go when the dog got in. I do not blame it. It was hungry, and it was on its own side of the hill. I would know it again." Your whole back has gone cold.

choices.text: Ask whether {he} still dreams of it

effects.log: "Only when I have eaten crab," {he} says, which is a joke of some kind. Then, a good while on: "I dream that I can run." You keep your face still, and you walk on the side of the leg from then on, in case {he} needs an arm.

choices.text: Ask what {he} would do if {he} met it

effects.log: "Walk round," {he} says. {He} thinks. "My uncle would do something else. We are that family. Did you not know? I keep the accounts, since this." {He} slaps the leg. You had not known. You had smelled it on {him}, all this time, and you took it for rain.

events.text: {npc} takes you home, up the valley. All five dogs go under the porch and stay there. The uncle, Dol-su, is sitting in the yard waxing a net, and stops. Dol-su has killed thirty-one tigers. The old man looks at the way you are standing, and at your feet, for some time. "Where are your people from?" says Dol-su, quite politely. There is a large pelt on the bench, and you are shown to it.

choices.text: Sit on it. Say, "Up the mountain." Eat what you are given

effects.log: You sit. It is a young female from the south range, and you nod to the pelt. You eat everything. The old man goes back to the net in the end, and every so often looks up. "Charcoal burners," says Dol-su. "Quiet people." Dol-su does not sound very sure.

choices.text: Remain standing. Thank the old man, and say that you do not sit on the dead

effects.log: There is a pause. The aunt puts down a dish. "Buddhists," says the aunt, in the tone of someone who has seen worse. {npc} laughs out loud. But the old man has stopped waxing, and is looking at you with something near to respect, which is bad.

events.text: The last night of the festival. Nearly everyone has gone. {npc} has stopped at the east corner, where {he} always stops, with the lantern low. "I know what they say about strangers who come down at this time of year," {he} says. "Walk one round with me, at this speed, and do not go on ahead. If you can do it, I will tell the family. If you cannot, I will not ask you again."

choices.text: Give {him} your arm. Walk it

effects.log: It takes until the bell. You do not go ahead, not by a toe. Your own legs are shaking with it when you get back to the corner. The monk on the steps has fallen asleep, and there is nobody else there to see it done, and it is done.

choices.text: You cannot. It is not in you. Tell {him}, and go up

effects.log: You say it, standing still. {He} nods. {He} goes on round, alone, and it is the only round that you have ever watched all the way to the end. You go up at dawn, a very long way, as fast as you have ever gone.

events.text: You cannot understand salt. They put it in everything. You eat what the house eats, and you go up by night with your whole stomach howling, and you are back by dawn, having dealt with it. You leave a deer in the yard. {npc} looks at the deer, which has nothing wrong with it but the neck. The uncle looks at it for longer. "That is good work," says the uncle. "Whose?" Everyone is suddenly very busy.

choices.text: Say it was yours. It is. Let them make what they like of it

effects.log: "Traps?" says the uncle. "Something of the kind," you say. The uncle cuts it up, slowly. There is a very good dinner, and you have never been looked at so thoroughly over one. Next month the uncle leaves a knife out for you, to see how you hold it.

choices.text: Stop leaving them. Learn to go hungry at the table

effects.log: It is a long winter. You get thin, and {npc} begins to worry, and to give you {his} fish. You have never in your life been given anything by something smaller. You are ashamed of how good it tastes.

events.text: Something is wrong with the family business. It has been five years since a man was taken on this side of the valley. You saw to that. You went and talked it over with the two man-eaters off the south range. The nets hang dry. The county has stopped paying, and the uncle sits in the yard with nothing to wax. {npc} is doing the accounts, and looking at you over them with one eyebrow up.

choices.text: Point out that nobody has been eaten

effects.log: "Yes," says {npc}. "It is a great blessing. We shall be selling the south field." {He} goes back to the numbers. It is a very curious thing to have saved people from being eaten and to have it entered as a loss.

choices.text: Let a few come over the ridge again, for the good of the house

effects.log: You look the other way for one spring. A tiger comes through and takes a calf, and only a calf. The county pays. The uncle is ten years younger, and goes singing up the valley, and {npc} watches you watch the old man go.

events.text: A monk from the capital is telling it at the temple gate, for the festival: the young man and the tiger maiden, and the three bad brothers, and how the maiden took the young man's blade in a bare hand, so that heaven would have one life, and the young man would have a rank. All the people are crying. You have been trying to work out what a rank is. {npc}, beside you, has stopped crying, and is looking at your hands.

choices.text: Ask {him}, going home, what {he} thinks of the maiden

effects.log: {He} goes quite a long way before {he} speaks. "I think that if you do that," {he} says, "I will not build you any temple. I will sit on the step with the accounts and I will be furious." You find that you are very glad to hear it.

choices.text: Say that it is a stupid story. No tiger would do it

effects.log: You say it too loudly. A woman turns round. {npc} takes your arm, and {he} leans on it, and you go on. "No," {he} says, "I do not suppose so. Most of them just shake you and let go." It is the first thing that {he} has ever said that hurt.

events.text: They bring it down the valley on a pole, with the whole village behind and the uncle in front, younger than you have ever seen the old man. You knew the tiger. That tiger had a torn ear, and once fought you over a boar and thought better of it. There is rice wine for everyone. {npc} comes out with a dish, and {he} puts it in your hands, and {he} sees your face, which you have forgotten to do anything about.

choices.text: Eat, at their table, with them. Then tell {him}, that night, in the dark

effects.log: You eat, and you drink their barley tea. You say what you are when the lamp is out, to the ceiling. There is nothing for a long time. "I know," {npc} says. "I know the name of the one with the torn ear, too, if you want it. I do the accounts." {He} takes your hand, and {his} own is very cold.

choices.text: Eat, and raise your teacup to the old man. Say nothing to anyone

effects.log: You raise your tea to the old man. The old man drinks to you. You help them with the pole. You go up that night, and you lie down where the tiger lay last, and you do not get up until morning. There will be another. You have decided that you can do this.

choices.text: Set the dish down on the ground, and walk out of that gate

effects.log: You do not hurry. Nobody stops you. The dogs come out from under the porch as you go, for the first time in years, and they begin to bark. {npc} stands in the yard with a full dish. By the time the moon is up, you are not anyone.

events.text: There is a rope on the path to the upper spring, and it was laid by someone who knows you. {npc}'s uncle has been reading your feet for fifteen years. The uncle sits on a stone by the path with a spear laid across the knees, in the blue dawn, an old man now. It has not been raised. "I would like to know," says the uncle, "before I am dead. I would take it as a kindness. You have been good to my {npc}."

choices.text: Take the shape. Stand on the path, and let the old man see

effects.log: You do it slowly, for an old man's eyes. You stand there, and you fill the path. The old man looks at you for a long time, with both hands quite still. "Well," says the old man. "Nineteen hands. I said eighteen." The spear stays down. The old man cries a little, and you do not know which of you it is for.

choices.text: Step over the rope, with your own two feet, and say good morning

effects.log: You step across it, as you might for a puddle. "Good morning," says the old man. A nod. The old man stays where the old man sits, and looks up at the sky. So that is how it will be. Neither of you is ever going to be the first one to speak, and you are both patient.

choices.text: Go up, past the old man, and do not come down

effects.log: You go straight up through the pines, and you let the old man see that. The old man does not get up. There is no one for {npc} to be angry at but an old man on a stone. You hear about it, years later, from a magpie, who has been waiting to tell you.

events.text: There is a child, {bk_child}, in the back room, in the fourth month. Every dog went under the porch on the night of it and came out very quiet. {npc} is sitting up, with {his} bad leg out, doing the sums for the midwife. They give it to you to hold. It has very large feet. It opens its mouth at you with no teeth in it at all, and it is the most frightening thing that you have ever been shown.

choices.text: Hold it the way you carried your own, by the loose of the neck

effects.log: There is a great outcry. You are given a lesson, with a folded cloth, in how it is done. You do not see the difference. It has gone to sleep at once, you point out, and nobody in that room thinks that this is a point in your favour.

choices.text: Hand it back, and go up and bring down something for {him} to eat

effects.log: It is a very large boar. They have to take down part of the gate. {npc} eats boar for nine days, and {he} walks again rather sooner than anyone said. The midwife will not come back, and the midwife tells people so.

events.text: New Year, and a second one, {bk_child}, so they want a painting on the gate. The man comes round with paper. A magpie in a pine, and under it a tiger, to frighten away all that is bad. You hold the corner, while {npc} nails it up. It has crossed eyes. It has a stupid soft grin and the feet of a cat. A magpie is explaining something to it. {npc} looks at this for a while, and at you, and {he} hits {his} thumb.

choices.text: Say that the stripes are wrong

effects.log: "You would know," says {npc}, with {his} thumb in {his} mouth. It stays up on that gate the whole of the year, looking at you. The baby likes it. In the end, you get so that you nod to it, coming home.

choices.text: Take it down by night, and do better, with a burnt stick

effects.log: It is not good. You have no hands for it. But you know what a tiger looks like when it has just seen something. It frightens all the children. {npc} looks at it in the morning, and {he} puts the other one back up. "We have to live here," {he} says.

events.text: {bk_child} is seven and has a dog. It is a poor yellow thing that came in out of the rain. It sleeps on {bk_child}'s feet, and it eats from that hand. Every other day of its life that dog has seen you and shaken from nose to tail, and tonight it looks at you across a sleeping seven-year-old with its lip up. It has made up its mind. {bk_love} sees it too, from the door, and starts to smile, with some effort.

choices.text: Walk round them, gladly, to get to your mat

effects.log: So you walk round. It watches you the whole way. Nothing is going to step off any path for that child, ever, and it will be bitten by things and shouted at by clerks, and it will have that dog.

choices.text: Lie down, on your side of the room, and look at the dog

effects.log: You look at it most of the night, without anything in your eyes at all. It is shaking badly by morning. Its lip is still up. You have killed a great many brave things, and you have to admit that you were not paying attention.

events.text: From the ridge you see it all, too far off. {bk_child}, seven, is coming home with sticks. On the path stands a thin old man-eater, and {bk_child} walks right up to it and stops, and looks it in the eye, and says one cross word. It steps off. It goes down the bank with its belly low. {bk_child} walks on. Then stops, looks back, and waits, for {bk_love} to come limping up the road, and takes it slowly from there.

choices.text: Go down and see to the man-eater. Then come home to dinner

effects.log: You catch up with it by dark. It does not trouble anyone again. You walk in with a clean face, and {bk_love} is ladling. Neither of you has anything to say. {bk_child} moves over on the mat, and you see that the feet have got no smaller.

choices.text: Tell {bk_love}, tonight, what you saw, and what it will cost

effects.log: You tell it all. Dogs and paths and rooms. Nobody will ever sit next to that child without being brave. {bk_love} goes on for a while with the mending. "One did," says {bk_love}. "It only wants someone who is slow." That is all the comfort there is, and it may be enough.

events.text: {npc} has been going round the pagoda again this spring. It takes {him} all night to do half of it. {He} sits at the east corner in the small hours, grey in the face. "I never did get up that mountain," {he} says. "Sixty years I have looked at it. I should have liked to see where you go." {He} says this quite calmly, to the lantern. There is nobody about. It is a very dark night, and you are a very large animal.

choices.text: Take the shape. Crouch down. Say, "Get on"

effects.log: You go up through the pines at the speed of a slow walk, and that is the hardest thing you have ever done. {His} hands are in your ruff. You stop at every place you know. {He} sees the sun come up from the top, and {he} says that it is overrated, and {he} is laughing, and {his} face is wet.

choices.text: Help {him} up, and walk the other half. At that speed. It is what you are for

effects.log: It takes the rest of the night. You have it down to an art by now. The monk is a different monk, and even that monk has been told about the two of you. {He} does not bring up the mountain again, and you carry that up there alone, like everything.

events.text: They bring {bk_love} up the valley road, very slowly, because that is how it is done. The bier goes at about the speed of a bad left leg. You see that from the pines, and you come down through them as you are. You walk along above the road, in plain sight of anyone who cares to raise their eyes, all the way to the hill. Some of them do. The old hunters do. Not one of them reaches for anything.

choices.text: Stay on the hill until the moon has gone round

effects.log: They find the marks in the spring, a slow track that goes round and round the mound and has worn quite deep. They do not say a word about it in the county, and the bounty on white skins is never collected in that valley.

choices.text: Go up. Go a long way up, and lay a very long hunt

effects.log: It lasts for a year, or more. You go as fast as you are able, and nothing on that mountain is ever slow enough. There are hills that you do not remember. When you come back, you are out of breath, and it is still spring there.

events.text: Some seventy years later there is a family in the valley towns who all walk alike. The grandfather does it and so do the small ones: a little swing of the left foot, from the hip. Nobody ever hurt them. It is only how they were taught to walk, by people who were taught. Ask them, and they will tell you that it is unlucky to hurry. And the dogs go very quiet where they pass, and {bk_child}'s name is on the gate.

choices.text: Walk down in the shape, once, and go past them at their pace

effects.log: You fall into it without thinking. A young one looks up at the stranger going by, swinging a left foot from the hip, and starts to say something, and for some reason does not. You are absurdly pleased, and you go home by the long way.

choices.text: Stay up on the ridge. Keep the pass clear on their market days

effects.log: A bad one comes over in the autumn, and it is quite surprised. Nothing has troubled that road on the fifth-day market for as long as anyone can remember. They put up a little stone to the mountain god, and it faces the wrong way.

events.text: One of {bk_child}'s people paints New Year gates, all up the coast, the worst in the province. It always comes out with crossed eyes and that terrible soft grin and the magpie at its ear. But if you look at it for long enough, it has one left hind foot just a little out of true. It sells very well, and nobody else will paint that foot. You take a good look at the magpie.

choices.text: Send the magpie down there with something to say about the feet

effects.log: It goes gladly. It sits on the painter's gate for a whole season and it screams about feet. The next year's are, if anything, worse. The foot stays where it is, and all down the coast they are saying that it is the lucky one.

choices.text: Lie across the road one evening, in your whole shape, for them to get it right

effects.log: They stop dead, with a brush behind one ear. They look at you for as long as they dare. Then they go home and paint it with crossed eyes. They do tell the family, though, that the stripes are correct, and they have the paper to prove it.

events.text: You walked three provinces to Howonsa, in the shape. It is a small place, with a leaky hall. {npc} cooks there, an old person of no vows at all, and {he} looks up from the pot when you come in. {He} looks at your feet. "That makes three this century," {he} says, "who have come to look at the temple. You are all so serious. Sit, you are making the cat ill. There is no meat." You find that you are sitting.

choices.text: Tell {him} about the left leg, and all of it, over the pot

effects.log: It takes three bowls. {He} goes on stirring. "And now you have got a stride like a tax collector with gout," {he} says, "and you would like someone to use it on." {He} ladles out another. "I have a bad hip. I go to market on the fifth." You had not asked.

choices.text: Finish the bowl. Thank {him}. Walk on, as fast as you like

effects.log: You go down the steps, and you find that you are going very slowly, and it takes some effort to stop. {He} stands in the door with a spoon, watching your feet. "That is not going to go away," {he} calls after you, cheerfully.

events.text: Someone is coming up the pass by themselves, at a slow walk, and all the tigers on your range are getting out of the way. This is a person of no great size. They stop at the cairn, a stone's throw from where you lie, and they look straight at the place. "Nobody walks with me," they say, not complaining. "I would be obliged, if you are going that way. As far as the spring."

choices.text: Get up, and go along. At that pace

effects.log: You go as far as the spring. They do not look at you, and nobody says anything else. It takes the afternoon. At the water they bow, and you drink, and they go back down by themselves, and all the tigers get out of the way again.

choices.text: Stay where you are, and let them see you decline

effects.log: They wait for a moment, and then nod, as if it were more or less what they had expected. They go on, swinging a left foot from the hip. You watch them to the top. It is not a thing you would care to do twice.

events.text: Dogs leave. You are six. They get up as you come in, not fast, and go out to the yard. At the well the other children all draw in their elbows and leave you the good side. It does not seem strange to you, until you see a boy shove another boy. {npc}, who knows the family, sees you watching. {He} comes over and shoves you, quite hard.

choices.text: Shove {him} back, and ask what that was for

effects.log: "That is for free," says {npc}. "Someone ought to, now and then." You have a bruise on your arm, and you are delighted with it, and you show it to everyone. They look at the bruise, and at you, and they do not come any nearer.

choices.text: Go out to the dog, and sit very still by it till it stays

effects.log: It takes all that summer. It never stops shaking, but it stays, and you think that this is what having a friend must be. {npc} brings you out some rice, and {he} sits on the other side of you, and {he} says nothing about the dog.

events.text: You are ten, and you have been taught to walk. It is a family thing: the little swing out from the left hip, and do not hurry, it is unlucky. Then you are late home one night, on the top road, and you meet something on it, long and low. You say, "Oh, get off," as you would to a calf. It goes down the bank. {npc} is on the road behind you, breathing hard, with a lantern and a hoe.

choices.text: Ask what that was

effects.log: {npc} looks at the bank for some time. "A large cat," {he} says. {He} puts the hoe over {his} shoulder. {He} is shaking so badly that the lantern rattles. You take it from {him}, and you carry it home, at the proper speed.

choices.text: Say nothing, and be early from now on

effects.log: You come home by the low road. You never say anything about it, and nor does {he}. But you lie awake on some nights feeling how far the top road is from your bed, and it does not seem very far.

events.text: A pot goes off the edge of the shelf, at the back of the kitchen. You are fourteen and on the other side of the room, with your back to it, and you are holding the pot. Nobody saw you cross. There is a gap in that moment, and you cannot find anything in it. The cook looks at you, and at the shelf. The cook takes the pot out of your hands with two fingers and puts it down. {npc} has stopped eating.

choices.text: Do it again, on purpose. Knock a spoon off

effects.log: You catch the spoon. You catch a bean. You are getting very good at it by autumn, out behind the barn, and {npc} comes and watches once, and says that a person who can do that should ask who it is that wants to know.

choices.text: Be clumsy. Drop some things, for a year or so

effects.log: You break three bowls that year. You have to watch each one all the way down, and it takes forever, and you can see the place where you would have caught it. Everyone is much friendlier. The cook gives you a slap and you could weep for joy.

events.text: You are sixteen, and you go up the mountain for firewood and you stay. You stop lighting a fire on the second night, and nothing comes near you, and on the fourth you notice that nothing has come near you for a very long way around. {npc} comes up on the sixth day with a bad wheeze. {He} looks at the clean ground. {He} gets down on a log, in stages. "Your feet," {he} says. "I had better tell you about your feet."

choices.text: Stay on the log, and hear it

effects.log: A pagoda on a festival night, and someone who walked too fast, and learned not to. A left leg that the family has been copying for two hundred years. A child called {bk_line}, and the one who is still up there, {bk_anc}. So that was the walk. You had thought it was manners.

choices.text: Tell {him} that you only came for wood

effects.log: You pick up your load. {npc} looks at it, and at you. You carry it down for the two of you at {his} speed. "Well, somebody will tell you," {he} says, at the gate. "I should like it not to be somebody with a net."

events.text: You go to the wine-house on the market road, because that is where people go. You sit down. By the second cup you have a bench to yourself. Nobody is rude. They just remember that they were meaning to stand over there. It is really a very friendly place, you can hear that much, all the way from here. {npc} comes in, and takes a long time to sit down beside you.

choices.text: Buy a round for the room, loudly, and go and sit in the middle

effects.log: They drink it. They raise their cups, and they laugh in the right places. Somebody tells you a good one. It is like being a very well liked magistrate. When you go, you can hear the whole room breathe out, and it sounds fond.

choices.text: Stay on your bench, and learn to like {npc}'s company

effects.log: {He} has very little to say, and most of it is about {his} knee. You come back the next week, and the one after that. You begin to see that there are people who would not call this a small thing.

events.text: The carters on the Sol pass have heard about you. The head carter, a broad person called Tae-man, comes by the house with a sack of millet and stands well back. There have been two taken this winter. Tae-man would be obliged if you would care to walk in front, this next trip, as far as the top. Just walking. {npc} looks at the millet, and shakes {his} head at you slowly.

choices.text: Walk in front. It is only a walk

effects.log: You swing along with a stick, for three days, with forty carts behind you, keeping their distance. Nothing stirs on the whole pass. It is the dullest thing you have ever done. They have your name on a post at the top now, and it does bring people to look at you.

choices.text: Say that you have a cough. Send them to the magistrate

effects.log: Tae-man takes back the millet, and looks rather relieved. Next winter there are three. You could not have been certain of anything, and you do not hear about that from anyone. You keep to the low road, and you keep going over the numbers.

events.text: Someone is calling you on the road home. It is your neighbour's voice, and it is calling your name. There is a small grey person in the wet ahead of you, with a bowl on its head, and you know that bowl: they turn a pot over on a cairn for these. It is a changgwi, and it has walked ahead of its tiger for a hundred years. It bows to you. "Where to, master?" it says. {npc} told you to run.

choices.text: Lead it to a cairn, and a pot. Tell it to go on home

effects.log: It takes all night, and it is very confused. It has forgotten the name of the place. You find a pile of stones on the Sol road. You set the pot over them, right way down, and you say the words, wrong. You are alone on the road at dawn, and your neck hurts.

choices.text: Tell it that it has the wrong person

effects.log: "Oh," it says. It looks at your feet. It bows a little lower. It walks on ahead of you along the road, to show that it understands. It is there on the next wet night, and it has been calling people, in your voice, for quite some way.

events.text: Tonight, going home, {npc} stops in the road. "You have been half a step behind me for all these years," {he} says. "I thought it was respect. But you have nothing wrong with your leg. I looked." {He} walks on three steps, then three more, faster, and you are half a step behind {him}. {He} is very quiet. "What are you doing that for? What are you holding back?"

choices.text: Show {him}. Walk at your own speed to the bend, and back

effects.log: It takes you no time. {He} has not finished blinking. {He} stands in the road and looks at the bend, and at you, with your hair not even moved. Then {he} takes your arm, and {he} is leaning on it quite hard. "Well, slow down, then," {he} says. "Who asked you?"

choices.text: Say it is an old family thing about the road and bad luck

effects.log: {He} looks at you, and {he} goes on. You stay half a step behind. It has never been a lie in any way that you could point to. You watch {his} heels the whole way home, as you always do, and you like them very much.

events.text: {npc} comes home from the village school with a clean face. {He} tells you, over {his} rice, about a boy called Gap-su, the big one, who always had the end of the bench. {He} went and stood in front of Gap-su. {He} did not do anything. {He} just stood there, and looked at the big boy, and Gap-su got up. Now {he} has the end of the bench. You put down your spoon.

choices.text: Take {him} out to the road, and teach {him} the walk. Tell {him} what it is for

effects.log: You walk {him} up and down until dark. You tell {him} who it was that first walked that way, and who for. {He} swings {his} foot out, rolling {his} eyes. The next day, {he} gives back the bench. {He} tells you this with the air of someone doing you a very large favour.

choices.text: Go and stand in front of {him}. Look at {him}. Wait

effects.log: {He} stops chewing. {He} goes a very odd colour. It lasts for about as long as you can stand it, and then you hold out the fish. Nobody at that table says one thing about it. {He} has not looked anybody in the eye since. You are not sure that you have done well.

events.text: {npc} sits down next to you in the wine-house. Next to you, on your bench, with {his} elbow against your elbow. Nobody has done that in your life. {He} has a tiger-catcher's tag, and an old grey dog raised on a skin, with no fear. The dog puts a grey head on your foot. "There," {he} says, and fills your cup. "Bori has been wanting to meet you. There is a lord in the capital who would pay a lot to be you."

choices.text: Get up, and show {him} how long it takes

ok.log: You have {him} by the collar, and the bench is on its side, and {he} never saw it. {He} laughs on the floor, delighted, with Bori licking {his} ear. "There!" {he} says. "That! I will be back," and you can see that {he} means it kindly.

fail.log: {He} has been waiting for that gap all {his} life, and {he} has a hook in it. You leave the place through a wall. You lie in a ditch all that night with your side open, and the dog comes and finds you, and the dog only sniffs, and goes home.

choices.text: Scratch the dog. Say that you are in grain. Stay on the bench

effects.log: You sit there with {him} for the rest of the evening, shoulder to shoulder, talking about grain. It is one of the best evenings of your life. {He} pays. "See you," {he} says, when {he} gets up, and Bori looks back from the door.

events.text: {npc} again, at the same bench, a long time later. {He} is very grey, and {he} has got no dog. "Bori died at the turn of the year," {he} says. "I have killed thirty-eight, and I have not sat next to anyone since you." {He} looks into {his} cup. "You had better know that I am going to try, since I told you I would. Shall we have one first?"

choices.text: Have one. Then go outside with {him}, and finish it

ok.log: It is over fast, on the frozen road. You sit down with {him}, after, in the snow, until {he} stops talking. {He} was telling you about the dog. Nobody comes near you. You pay for the two cups. {He} had Bori's collar in {his} sleeve, and you keep that.

fail.log: {He} knows you by now. {He} puts you down at the second step, and {he} stands over you with the hook, wheezing, and {he} does not use it. "No," {he} says, and {he} sits. "Later. I am tired." {He} is there on the bench in the morning, and you both know.

choices.text: Buy the jar. Tell {him} no, and that you will sit here as long as {he} likes

effects.log: {He} looks at you for some time. "That is not how it is done," {he} says. You pour. You sit up all night, the two of you, and in the morning {he} has gone, and has left {his} hook on the bench, and the bill. You do not hear of {him} again.

events.text: You wake up on the ridge with no shoes on. It is a good ten li from your bed, and very cold, and you are not cold. There are tracks in the frost, and they go round the place where you were lying: one set, very wide, walking round and round you, all night, the way that people go round a pagoda. {npc} is coming up through the trees with your shoes. {He} stops at the edge of the tracks.

choices.text: Put your foot in one, and walk the round

effects.log: It takes you the rest of the morning, for your stride is not half of what it wants. By the end of it, your back has stopped hurting for the first time since you were a child. {npc} is still there, holding out your shoes. {He} has got them the wrong way round.

choices.text: Put on your shoes, and walk down, and bar the door

effects.log: You bar it. You sleep with your shoes on and the bar across, and {npc} sits up. There are no more tracks. Only a dent in the frost on the far side of your own fence, as big as a door, where something has been lying.

events.text: Food has stopped tasting. Rice is warm, and salt is nothing. Tonight there is a good smell somewhere, and you are in the yard of the Cha house at moonrise, standing in front of the ox stall with your mouth wet. The ox knows. It is an old ox, and it is trying to get through the back wall. {npc} is behind you. {He} sounds very calm.

choices.text: Go up. Tonight, and for as long as it takes

effects.log: You walk straight up the hill. It is seven days before you come down, thin and calm and with your hands clean. Rice has a taste now, a little. You do not say what you have been doing, and {npc} does not ask, and the Chas still have their ox.

choices.text: Turn round. Go in and eat the rice. Eat all of it

effects.log: You eat with {npc} watching. It is like eating warm sand. You eat it the next night too, and the whole of that year, at the table with the rest, and it never does begin to taste. But the ox lives to be very old, and you bring it greens.

events.text: {npc} brings you to the pagoda, for the last night of the festival, when nearly everyone has gone. "It comes," {he} says, and sits down on the steps. You go round, with the family walk. There is someone going round the other side of the stone, all in white, or it is the moon. They pass you once, like a wind. Then they are at your left hand, and they have slowed right down. It is {bk_anc}, or what is left.

choices.text: Keep walking, side by side, at your speed. Do not look

effects.log: You do three whole rounds. Nothing is said. There is a very large warmth at your left hand, and no breath. At the east corner it stops, as if somebody were resting. You rest. When the bell goes, there is one line of very deep prints.

choices.text: Stop at the east corner. Bow, and let it go on by

effects.log: You bow. It goes on by. You stay down until your back aches. You can hear no footsteps, but all of the lanterns on that side lean over and come upright again. {npc} says nothing on the road home. It seems you did it properly.

events.text: You have been sent for. There is a magpie on your gate saying so. You go up the mountain, with {npc} waiting at the last cairn. There is a dry cave, swept clean by something large. At the back of it, on a shelf of rock, is a walking stick. It is very old. The grip has been worn down by a hand, and then, on top of that, for a long time after, by teeth. Up on the ledge, {bk_anc} does not stir.

choices.text: Leave it where it is. Sit down with it for a while

effects.log: You sit for the rest of the day. Nobody has told you what this is, and nobody needs to. When you go, you look at the ledge. You could not swear that there is anything there, or that there has been for years.

choices.text: Take it down, and walk out with it. Somebody ought to use it

effects.log: It fits your hand. You cannot think why. Nothing stops you, though you feel something watching all the way down to the cairn. {npc} sees it, and {he} goes quite white. You go on down the hill, swinging your left foot out, and leaning on it.

events.text: A dog walked up to you last week, and looked at you, and lay down dead of it. You are spending more nights up there than down here. {npc} has come to the last cairn, as far as {he} can. "Two speeds will tear you," {he} says. There is a temple cure, for the possessed and such, and it would take the mountain out of you. Or you could go on up. There is one other way, but nobody has walked that slowly in years.

choices.text: Have it taken out. Sit with people, and be shoved

effects.log: It takes a hundred days in a cold room, with a monk who does not like you. When you come out, you are a great deal smaller, and a passing cart driver shouts at you to get out of the road. You thank the driver, with tears in your eyes.

choices.text: Go on up. Leave your shoes on the cairn

effects.log: You set them down side by side, facing home. {npc} takes them. You go up at your own speed, and it is the first time in your life, and you are out of sight before {he} has straightened up. You had not known that it could be so fast.

choices.text: Keep both. Hunt the ridge, and be home for the market

effects.log: It takes more slowing down than anybody has ever had to do. {npc} looks at your shoes, and says that it can be done, because somebody once went up a mountain at the speed of a bad leg, and nothing tore.

events.text: A yellow dog bites you in the market on your first morning out. It is a hard, honest bite in the calf, and you are shouting and hopping and people are laughing. You have never been so happy. A woman tells you to mind where you are going, and elbows you out of the way. {npc} has to help you home. Now you do have a limp, and nobody had to teach it to you.

choices.text: Go back, and make friends with the dog

effects.log: It bites you twice more. You take it a bone every day, and by the winter it will sit near you. It is not afraid of you in the least. It simply has no opinion. You could not have asked for more.

choices.text: Go to the wine-house, and sit in a crowd until they tell you to move up

effects.log: "Move up," someone says, and gives you a shove. You move up. Somebody's elbow is in your soup. You stay there until they shut, and you are told that you are a bore, and you ask them to say it again.

events.text: They leave things on the last cairn now: a bowl, a shoe, some rice, a piece of paper with a tiger on it, cross-eyed. You have no need of any of it. {npc} has been up with a bowl, as far as the bad hip will go. You lie in the pines above and watch {him} set it down, and straighten up, and go off down the road, at that terrible speed. You do not know why you are walking along.

choices.text: See {him} to the bottom, from the trees, every time

effects.log: It takes half a day, and you have things to kill. {He} never looks round. Once, at the turning, {he} says "Thank you" to a bush, in the wrong direction, quite politely, and goes on.

choices.text: Keep to the high range, where it is cleaner

effects.log: It is very clean. It is the finest hunting in the country, and you run down what you please. Nobody on the high range walks at any speed but yours. The bowls go on being put out, you hear. A magpie told you, and it was laughing.

events.text: You keep shoes under a stone at the tree line. On market days you come down, and you limp up and down the rows buying salt, which you still cannot understand. In the evenings you are up on the ridge. {npc} says that the hens have stopped laying, and that it is your fault. The carters have started to leave a jug at the tree line. They do not ask, and you do not always bring back the jug.

choices.text: Keep the pass, and take the jug

effects.log: There has not been a bad year on that road for as long as you have been at it. They think that it is the post they put up. You have a good look at the post, sometimes. Your name is spelled wrong.

choices.text: Take a day off from both. Sit on the stone with your shoes off

effects.log: You do nothing all day. A magpie comes along to tell you what it thinks of this. Below you, the market goes on, and above you, the mountain does. There is hardly anyone in the country who knows how to do this, and you are bad at it.

events.text: You are old, and the small ones are being taught the walk. You have a bad hip now, a real one, and so at last you do it without trying. One of them has it quite wrong, and goes out from the right. {npc} is telling that one to do it properly. "Why?" says the child. "It is unlucky to hurry," says {npc}. The child looks at you, across the yard, and you look back. Then the child goes down to the gate at a run.

choices.text: Laugh until you cough. Let that one be

effects.log: It will have some bad falls, and some good days. You see it go by the gate at full tilt, with a stick, and the dogs getting out of the way. Someone will have to slow that one down. Somebody always comes along.

choices.text: Call it back, and show it. Slowly. Tell it who for

effects.log: It comes back, and stands there, kicking the step. You tell it about a person with a lantern, who did not draw in their elbows. It listens with half an ear. Then it swings its left foot out, once, to see, and then again.

events.text: They carry you up to the first cairn this last autumn, because you have asked them to. {npc} stops the bearers when they get to the place. You have spent a whole life being given the good side of every road, and you look round now at all these people, standing quite close to you, because they have to, to hold the poles.

choices.text: Ask them to set you down, and go on standing there

effects.log: They stand. Someone's elbow is against your ear. It is an awkward, sweaty crowd, and none of them is drawing back. Far up on the hill, something large has stopped walking, to look. You take your time.

choices.text: Have them take you up one more bend, at the family speed

effects.log: It takes the rest of the day. They complain all the way, and they swing their left feet. You have never in your life gone anywhere at any better pace. When they stop for the night, you can see the whole valley, and it is overrated.
